title: Paul Bettany Says He and Johnny Depp ‘Hadn’t Spoken’ in Years When Their Texts Were Read During Libel Trial: ‘I Was Being Painted As This Close Friend’
description: Paul Bettany opened up in a recent interview with The Times about the public’s misconception of his relationship with Johnny Depp after text messag
body:
Paul Bettany opened up in a recent interview with The Times about the public’s misconception of his relationship with Johnny Depp after text messages between the two actors were used in court during Depp’s libel lawsuit against The Sun.

	“I hadn’t spoken to Johnny in years when that happened and I haven’t spoken to him since. I was being painted as this close friend of a guy I hadn’t spoken to in years and, honestly, amid all the shit two celebrities threw at each other, that bit was the most odd,” Paul told the publication. 
	

	“So I decided to say nothing because, I think, people know me,” he continued. “I’ve been married 23 years and, for what I do, I live an incredibly quiet life. Everybody kind of thought this is probably a nothing burger – and left it alone.”

	In 2013, a controversial text exchange between Depp and Bettany became public when it was read during a Feb. 2020 trial hearing. “Let’s burn Amber!!!” wrote Depp, to which Bettany responded: “Having thought it through I don’t think we should burn Amber – she’s delightful company and easy on the eye, plus I’m not sure she’s a witch. We could of course try the English course of action in these predicaments ­– we do a drowning test. Thoughts?” Depp responded that they should “drown her before we burn her!!! I will fuck her burnt corpse afterwards to make sure she’s dead.”

	The two actors worked together on multiple films, including 2010’s “The Tourist,” 2014’s “Transcendence” and 2015’s “Mortdecai.”

	Depp initially sued News Group Newspapers (NGN) (which publishes The Sun) for libel after an article was published by the publication titled “Gone Potty – How can JK Rowling be ‘genuinely happy’ casting wife beater Johnny Depp in the new ‘Fantastic Beasts’ film?” Depp alleged that the article “caused serious harm to (his) personal and professional reputation” and also caused him “significant distress and embarrassment.” In 2020, Judge Andrew Nicol ruled against Depp.

schema.headline: Paul Bettany Says He and Johnny Depp ‘Hadn’t Spoken’ in Years When Their Texts Were Read During Libel Trial: ‘I Was Being Painted As This Close Friend’

title: Gene Schwam, Veteran Hollywood Publicist to Elvis Presley, Julie Andrews and More, Dies at 96
description: Veteran Hollywood publicist Gene Schwam, who represented top talent including Elvis Presley, Blake Edwards, Julie Andrews, Barbara Eden and Lenny B
body:
Veteran Hollywood publicist Gene Schwam, who represented top talent including Elvis Presley, Blake Edwards, Julie Andrews, Barbara Eden and Lenny Bruce, died Friday in Los Angeles after a brief illness. He was 96.

	Schwam co-founded Hanson & Schwam Public Relations with Adeline Hanson in 1955, establishing an independent publicity agency that would endure for decades.

	Schwam was earning $35 a week working for publicist Stanley Cowan when he decided to strike out on his own. He joined forces with Hanson, a part-time disc jockey and publicist, to launch their firm. When it came time to decide whose name would come first, Schwam wanted his own name at the front. Hanson’s response settled the matter: “Ladies first.”
	

	Starting with Smith Bros. Fish Shanty restaurant as their first client, Hanson & Schwam grew into an enduring presence in entertainment publicity, with Schwam continuing as president and co-founder decades later. 


	Clients included Nancy Wilson and Lou Rawls, as well as the famous Coconut Grove nightclub, which helped the agency foster relationships with numerous entertainers.

	His colorful representation (and intentional misreputation) of Presley in 1957 was covered in Variety at the time of the release of Baz Luhrmann’s “Elvis” in 2022.Schwam’s longtime relationship with Edwards extended beyond the professional. He was a friend as well as a publicist to the legendary director of such classics as “Breakfast at Tiffany’s,” “10,” and“Victor/Victoria.”

	Edwards’ character of the neurotic publicist in his film “S.O.B.” was based on Schwam. That friendship reflected something fundamental about Schwam’s approach: he was known for his passionate engagement and resourceful guidance of his clients’ careers.

	Vernon Scott, the longtime United Press International entertainment correspondent, called him “The best idea man in Hollywood,” a description that captured the inventive thinking at the center of Schwam’s work. 
	

	Later in life, Schwam created Humanity 101, an initiative of Arizona State University’s Project Humanities, promoting the values of compassion, empathy, forgiveness, integrity, kindness, respect and self-reflection.

	He is survived by his wife, Myrna; daughter Stephanie Schwam (Instagram contact @youreprettyandnice); stepchildren Adam, Greg and Linda London; and five grandchildren.

schema.headline: Gene Schwam, Veteran Hollywood Publicist to Elvis Presley, Julie Andrews and More, Dies at 96

title: ‘Musk’ TikTok Account Permanently Suspended Ahead of Documentary’s Wide Release
description:
TikTok permanently suspended the “Musk” ad account on Friday ahead of the documentary’s wide release, Variety can confirm.  

	Directed by Alex Gib
body:
TikTok permanently suspended the “Musk” ad account on Friday ahead of the documentary’s wide release, Variety can confirm.  

	Directed by Alex Gibney, “Musk” seeks to make sense of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, and the outsized influence he has on the world, diving deep into his shift to MAGA supporter, controversies surrounding his Occupy Mars mission and Tesla’s self-driving cars and his contentious relationships with several of the mothers of his 14 children.
	

	The documentary opened in a limited release in New York and Los Angeles on Oct. 9, grossing $68,900 from four locations (an average of $17,225 per screen) before expanding to 472 North American theaters on Friday. The documentary made about $120,000 on Friday and is expected to reach $385,000 by Sunday, per estimates from rival studios.


	Reps for TikTok did not immediately reply to Variety‘s requests for comment. 

	Even beyond the film’s account suspension on TikTok, the 3-hour-and-45-minute has already faced it’s fair share of controversy ahead of its release. In an interview with The New York Times, Gibney confirmed that Universal Pictures wavered in planning the doc’s overseas release. When questioned about what happened, Gibney responded: “Were they concerned that in this political environment, a film about the world’s richest man was problematic? Maybe, but you have to ask them.” (Legal threats from the SpaceX founder initially raised audience concerns about an international release.)

	Ahead of the film’s release, Musk called it a “hit piece” and said “dogshit is worth more respect.” He added that Gibney “has ZERO integrity” and is a “horrible human.”
	

	The Hollywood Reporter was the first to report the news.

schema.headline: ‘Musk’ TikTok Account Permanently Suspended Ahead of Documentary’s Wide Release

title: ‘Klara and the Sun’ Review: There’s No Life — Intelligent, Artificial or Otherwise — in Taika Waititi’s Calamitous Android Fantasy
description: Adapting a solemnly complex, questioning novel as a cockeyed child’s-eye comedy worked once before for Taika Waititi — which is to say that “Jojo R
body:
Adapting a solemnly complex, questioning novel as a cockeyed child’s-eye comedy worked once before for Taika Waititi — which is to say that “Jojo Rabbit,” his crass, mawkish “anti-hate satire” about a Hitler Youth member’s personal and political awakening, won him an Oscar and grossed nearly $100 million, in spite of its manifold artistic and ethical shortcomings. But even that film’s many defenders are unlikely to be moved in sizable numbers by his twee, pulseless fantasy “Klara and the Sun” — such a hopeless mismatch of filmmaker and source material, it appears to be have been assembled as a kind of perverse defy-the-odds challenge. Whether there was ever a successful movie to be made of Kazuo Ishiguro’s finespun, melancholic, almost brittly interior study of android consciousness is open to question, but Waititi should reasonably be in the bottom tier of auteurs you’d enlist to try, maybe just ahead of Baz Luhrmann, but a notch below Quentin Tarantino.
	

	Published in 2021, “Klara and the Sun” is a confidently delicate novel, skirting slightness — as well as a bit of thematic recycling — in the way that a recent Nobel laureate can afford to do. It reads as something of a companion piece to “Never Let Me Go,” Ishiguro’s sober, mournful study of a human clone reflecting on her place in a hostile universe; swap in AI robots for clones, and “Klara” plows much the same field. “Never Let Me Go” got a fitting adaptation in Mark Romanek’s chilly, elegant 2010 drama of the same title; that film couldn’t have been more stylistically coordinated to the author’s voice, and you’d hardly expect the director of “What We Do in the Shadows” and two “Thor” movies to take the same approach.
	

	But from the very first tinkly strains of Michael Giacchino’s overbearingly precious score, it’s obvious that moist-eyed whimsy is an ill-chosen path; the filmmaker’s variously cutesy, kooky affectations fight the stoic sadness of Ishiguro’s storytelling at every turn. (The author takes an executive producer credit, and one would give several pennies for his thoughts.) Having premiered at London after being conspicuously absent from September’s season-launching festivals, “Klara and the Sun” will open in theaters on October 23, and looks to have all the cultural staying power of a standard ChatGPT conversation — with any audiences that do turn up likely to be nonplussed by a fable that’s pitched too juvenile for adults, and way too dull for children. 

	The comedy is broadest, and therefore most strikingly unfunny, in an opening section that plays as a ghastly dystopian update of “Annie” — introducing Ortega’s perma-sparkly Klara as one of several lonely humanoid AFs (artificial friends) awaiting human purchase in a store managed in tough-love fashion by a hard-mugging Natasha Lyonne. We are some way into a post-Third World War future where the internet has collapsed and people are largely housebound; the wealthy buy AFs to keep their isolated, unsocialized children company. Not that you get much sense of this reality — or any reality at all, really — from Michael Berlucchi’s textureless, aggressively gold-filtered lensing or Ra Vincent’s daintily retro production design, least of all in Lyonne’s midcentury-style Friend Store: Humanity already appears to be occupying a floaty simulacrum of the way things were.

	Ortega, button-cute amid the eeriness of everything else, never bursts into a rendition of “Tomorrow,” but she does open the film with a winsome monologue thanking the sun for her existence — she is solar-powered, after all — and praying to the godly orb for a loving buyer, so close enough. She finally gets her wish when sullen teen Josie (promising British talent Mia Tharia, recently seen in “The Education of Jane Cumming”) spots her in the shop window, is beguiled by her visible quirkiness (she stands on one leg, for starters) and persuades her uptight mother Chrissy (Amy Adams, as prim and hard as the string of pearls around her neck) to bring the robot girl home to their isolated and wholly unbelievable Midwest-ish farmhouse.
	

	There, Klara’s attempts to fit into a dysfunctional human household yield some halting fish-out-of-water hijinks, as she rubs both Chrissy and brusque Kiwi housekeeper Melania (Rachel House) the wrong way, while enchanting Josie with her open heart and ingenuous curiosity. But here, the film’s tonal balance begins tipping toward tragedy, over which Waititi has no more command than its flatlining comedy: Josie, it emerges, has a life-threatening illness, which puts Klara in a rather more crucial position in the family than anyone initially dared to admit. And so the script — written by Waititi with TV vet Dahvi Waller (“Mrs. America”) in her first big-screen credit — blunders into existential explorations of artificial life and afterlife that any number of recent, comparably lo-fi works, from “Ex Machina” to “Marjorie Prime” to “Her” to “Robot Dreams,” have probed with more nuance and wit.

	Ortega, innately charismatic as ever, tries to make Klara enough of a life force to give these conflicts and considerations some weight, but is defeated by the one-note writing of her character as a relentlessly hopeful, Pollyanna-esque naif. The story’s later stages hinge on Klara’s faltering, increasingly shattered digital memory, but save for some glitching, strikingly pixelated graphics, we never get a vivid sense of how she actually sees the world. Not that her human counterparts feel any richer or realer, with Adams particularly script-trapped as the stiffly guarded Chrissy, who shoulders enough grief, both lingering and preemptive, to match the actor’s “Arrival” character, yet never gets to give it satisfying expression.

	Ishiguro’s novel was plainspoken in its pathos, as has always been the author’s gift: His characters carry the disappointments and more crushing losses of their lives as part of their everyday routine, often acknowledging and dismissing them in the same simple sentence. Waititi’s writing, even in its best vehicles, has no such piercing gift. He aims to smuggle feeling in through irony and farce, intrusions that here curdle unhappily with the heartsore earnestness of the source. If there were any more life to the filmmaking, this tension could least be interesting, but the results are both perky and inert, unreal but entirely unmoored in time and space. As desperate to be loved as its beaming heroine, but far more knowingly so, Waititi’s “Klara and the Sun” is a warmly worded Hallmark card from an artificial friend.

schema.headline: ‘Klara and the Sun’ Review: There’s No Life — Intelligent, Artificial or Otherwise — in Taika Waititi’s Calamitous Android Fantasy

title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Pulls Val Chmerkovskiy After ‘Inappropriate’ Carrie Ann Inaba Slap Joke: ‘The Well-Being’ of Our Staff Is ‘Non-Negotiable’
description:
“Dancing With the Stars” is benching Val Chmerkovskiy after his recent joke about judge Carrie Ann Inaba.

	“The well-being of everyone who works o
body:
“Dancing With the Stars” is benching Val Chmerkovskiy after his recent joke about judge Carrie Ann Inaba.

	“The well-being of everyone who works on ‘Dancing with the Stars’ is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show,” BBC Studios said in a statement on Saturday. “As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.”


	Chmerkovskiy shared a statement of his own following the announcement that he will not be in the ballroom, writing on Instagram, “In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention. Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was.”
	

	He continued, “The last thing I want is to become a distraction from an important week or from the incredible work my dance partner Jenna Dewan is putting in. Please send Carrie Ann, Jenna, and the whole DWTS family lots of love during Dedication Night. I’ll be watching and cheering everyone on!!”



	

									Disney
	



	For context, during the Oct. 13 episode of “Dancing With the Stars,” judge Carrie Ann Inaba critiqued Jenna Johnson (who is married to Chmerkovskiy) for having a lift in her routine, and read her the definition of said lift. Afterward, Chmerkovskiy posted to his TikTok story, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” seemingly referencing Will Smith slapping Chris Rock at the 2022 Oscars, after saying, “Keep my wife’s name out of your fucking mouth.”
	

	The post was quickly deleted, but Inaba saw it and commented on her own Instagram, thanking the media for alerting her to his remark.

	Chmerkovskiy, who has appeared on “Dancing With the Stars” since the second season, later apologized to Inaba and the viewers he upset, posting the following message on his Instagram Story on Thursday: “I want to apologize from the bottom of my heart for my recent post. I have reached out to Carrie Ann to apologize directly and personally, and I also want to apologize publicly as I understand my words affect so many outside of our internal DWTS family. I recognize that l am in a fortunate position to have a platform and to be a role model to some, and I need to treat that with more care by actively pausing to think before I post to ensure what I am sharing aligns with who l am, and who I want to be for you all. I am truly sorry to Carrie Ann, and everyone who I hurt with my careless post. I will do better moving forward.”

	Jenna Dewan, Chermkovskiy’s partner, will still dance at dedication week, Variety confirms, and will be paired with Alan Bersten, who was eliminated in week three. Dewan will be dancing a Viennese waltz to “Unchained Melody,” dedicated to her mother.

	“Jenna Dewan is aware and has continued to be a true professional and respectful of the process,” the source tells Variety. “Jenna is a beloved part of the ‘Dancing with the Stars’ family, and we are grateful for the joy and positivity she brings to the show.”

	During Season 34, Inaba opened up to Variety about the criticism and constant booing she receives in the ballroom — something the male judges, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli, do not.

	“It used to really affect me. I have been targeted with this kind of negativity since the show began, back when we had chat rooms. I remember seeing some horrible words written about me, and I was shocked,” she shared. “Sometimes the things they say are cruel, and that has affected me. It’s made me scared. It’s not so much that I get hurt as I get afraid, because it feels like they’re attacking me verbally, so I shrink down a little during the season, especially after week five or six.”

schema.headline: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Pulls Val Chmerkovskiy After ‘Inappropriate’ Carrie Ann Inaba Slap Joke: ‘The Well-Being’ of Our Staff Is ‘Non-Negotiable’

title: How ‘Whalefall’ Production Designer Ramsey Avery Built the Creature’s Stomach Using Mattress Foam and Silicone Bits
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “Whalefall,” out now in theaters.

	In the new feature “Whalefall,” Jay (Austin Abrams) is a
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “Whalefall,” out now in theaters.

	In the new feature “Whalefall,” Jay (Austin Abrams) is a grieving son searching for his father’s (Josh Brolin) remains off the coast of California. As he dives deeper, Jay encounters a giant squid being chased by an 80-foot, 60-ton sperm whale. When the goliaths of the ocean battle it out, Jay finds himself sucked into the whale just as the squid’s tentacles wrap around him, proving to be a force he can’t contend with. Jay finds himself in the belly of the whale with only an hour’s worth of oxygen left as he fights to find his way out.
	

	What follows is an intense, anxiety-driven and claustrophobic adventure, with Brolin’s voice and flashbacks guiding Jay along the way.


	“It’s an intense experience, and that’s what we were going for,” says the film’s production designer Ramsey Avery. 

	Avery achieved that because he created practical whale sets, including a 30-foot whale head with a functional tongue mounted on an animatronic arm, allowing it to open and close. Filming in water and in camera using practical effects provided additional challenges, with the design of the set varying depending on where inside the whale Jay was located. The process began with extensive research.

	Research



	

	



	Avery started by examining autopsy photos of sperm whales and working closely with Dr. Joy Reidenberg, a biomedical research scientist. “She shared with me autopsies in the morning. I would get up at 6 a.m., look at autopsies with her as she was cutting open whales and explaining things to me.”
	

	But that still didn’t give him a sense of what the inside of a whale’s stomach looked like when it was alive and in water. 

	“We found out very quickly that we don’t know very much. But we do have cameras going into the bellies of orcas, dolphins and porpoises, so we were able to start with that and see what they look like when they’re filled with fluids and when they’re moving.”

	Building the Whale



	

	



	Avery began with the key stomach set, which he calls “stomach number one.” This is where Jay spends most of his time. Director Brian Duffield wanted everything to be in water, so Avery built a 60-foot-wide tank that was 20 feet deep. “We ended up building about 30 feet of the whale’s head that we could put into the tank, and it had an articulating mouth and we could move it forward on a ram and back.” 

	He collaborated with the stunts team and rigging team, as well as the film’s cinematographer Aaron Morton, to understand what he needed. “We pushed as much of it being practically in-camera as we could,” says Avery. The tongue in the back of the whale’s throat was also a physical build, capable of moving up and down.

	Finding the right material to construct the stomach was a challenge and required exploration. “It’s upholstery foam,” Avery reveals. “It’s two to three inches depending on where it is.”

	The interior was made of multiple layers of translucent, colored silicone to create a viscous look. The exterior was covered with heavy-duty canvas and coated with glue for added rigidity, while still allowing flexibility. “This made the stomach look alive,” Avery explains.

	The finished product required some additional digital effects work with Weta Workshop, but ultimately was “strong enough that it stood up for Jay being in it with water and stunt guys and camera and visual and special effects for six weeks.” Avery reveals the claustrophobia feeling comes from the inside. “The inside of the stomach is about eight feet wide and six feet tall when fully expanded,” Avery says. “Most of the time, though, it’s the size of a sleeping bag. It’s tight — just enough room for Jay and one or two cameras.”

	Rigs and Movement

	To simulate the motion of the whale, Avery experimented with different techniques. At first, he thought of using pistons on the outside or using ropes. But when they needed the whale to rise or dive, it couldn’t be done. “We had four different stomachs on different rigs to make that happen,” Avery says. “Our main stomach was on a small rig that always kept the whale in motion and swimming.” And there was a spinning rig that was like a washing machine for when the whale would spin.
	



	

	



	Stomach Bile

	In one sequence of the film, Jay finds himself in the whale’s stomach bile. All the colors depicted inside the whale were based on real-life anatomy. “The back of the throat is white, and the first stomach — the chewing stomach — is muscular and white with some pink tones,” Avery explains. “The second stomach, with its red acids, is pink.” These colors also mirrored Jay’s emotional journey. “He’s going from something that feels somewhat OK to ‘I don’t want to be here. This is a horrible place to be.’”

	Creating the stomach’s viscous bile was another challenge. “Brian [Duffield] wanted it to feel like a slog for Jay to move through, like he really had to work,” Avery says. To achieve this, the team used methyl cellulose (a thickening agent) mixed with various additives to create a texture similar to oatmeal. They also manufactured silicone bits and pieces to simulate floating debris in the water and added bubble ports to mimic the effect of acid eating away at objects. 

	Avery explains, “All of this was placed on a large teeter-totter rig. That allowed us to create big, sloshing movements to make it look like the whale was diving and the stomach acids were churning around Jay.”

title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Costume Designer on Blending Historical Accuracy and Modern Styling for the Dashwood Sisters: ‘We Want to Do Jane Austen Justice’
description: “Sense and Sensibility” costume designer Grace Snell thought in chapters for Georgia Oakley’s new take on Jane Austen’s 1811 novel, starring Daisy
body:
“Sense and Sensibility” costume designer Grace Snell thought in chapters for Georgia Oakley’s new take on Jane Austen’s 1811 novel, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, respectively.

	The most distinct chapters, from Snell’s costuming perspective, are the country and the city. First, the Barton Cottage chapter, shaped by the Devonshire landscape. There, behind closed doors, the relationship between the Dashwood sisters is at its most intimate. Then, the London chapter, where Elinor and Marianne’s presentation to society takes on a different palette. Snell says the sets, weather and changing seasons inspired her work in the different phases.
	

	Austen’s debut novel begins with the Dashwood family — sisters Elinor, Marianne, Margaret and their mother — settled at Norland Park, their Sussex estate. It’s set between the Georgian and Regency eras, in what Snell calls an “unusual transition period” as fashion began to “massively revolutionize” into the simpler style associated with Austen. Snell’s costuming inspiration, however, pulls from an array of eras, from period-accurate paintings and archival costume pieces to family portraits from the 2000s.


	In those photographs, “I really homed in on the intimacy that is within a family,” Snell says. “Particularly with sisters, and how relaxed and how comfortable they are with each other, and what that looks like in clothing.”

	One of Snell’s favorite details, and one she hopes fans pick up on, is that the sisters share clothing — emphasized by the Dashwood girls’ age gap. At the onset, Marianne is 19, Elinor is 16 and Margaret is 13.
	

	“There’s moments of borrowing because that’s what sisters do. They’re stealing clothes from each other. There’s being inspired by each other and reimagining clothing,” Snell says. “The dynamic of those sisters and how they share clothes and how they’re inspired by each other was important. We do rework some of the fabrics so that the garments look that they have a life themselves and how garments are loved and shared and borrowed within a family.”



	

					Illustration by Ruby Enticknap
									Grace Snell
	



	Inspired by those family photographs from the early aughts, as well as some runway looks from the ‘80s and ‘90s, Snell styled the film with a more modern take. Part of that was based on a desire to make the period piece feel more accessible.

	“What I wanted to do was design a film that I could see myself in, my friends in, my family in, try and knock down the wall that often is associated with period dramas,” Snell explains. “There’s sometimes this level of separation that you feel you’re looking at them on a pedestal, and I really wanted to open that up.”

	Still, “Sense and Sensibility” is not a modern film. Snell, who studied historical dress at university, brought a dress historian on board for three weeks of research. “I wanted how we made the costumes to be historically accurate with the fabrics we used, and the techniques we used, and the hand sewing,” she says. “For me as a designer, it was an amazing experience to try and fight those two sides, making historic accuracy marry up with how I wanted to give us a more modern take in the film.”

	The film’s colors were also chosen with care: “Sense and Sensibility” begins in a period of mourning, which formed “this idea of ‘shades of black.’” When the Dashwood sisters are in London, Elinor and Edward are both in shades of blue to reflect the disappointment of their situation. Snell used brighter colors in controlled ways, mainly for the supporting characters.



	

					Illustration by Ruby Enticknap
									Grace Snell
	



	“Sense and Sensibility” was Snell’s first period film, and she says part of the challenge was simply the volume of pieces. At the same time, she had to manage the entire costume team. There’s a lot to juggle, so the first challenge “is within yourself and your own head,” she says. “The biggest challenge is overcoming self-doubt.”
	

	Snell is a self-proclaimed Austen fan, so she understood how much of an undertaking this adaptation was. “I tried to not be intimidated by the fact that we were making a Jane Austen and how big a deal that was,” she says.

	This film looks different from Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation, which Snell notes is a touchstone for many Austen fans. “I love that film. I have massive respect for [costume designers] Jenny Beavan and John Bright,” she says. But “it was not a reference point for the design. They were two separate things, but the weight of how much it’s a beloved film, obviously we have to acknowledge that there are going to be people that that is a film that has meant so much to them.”

	Rather than referring back to Lee and Emma Thompson, Snell brings it back to Austen herself. “We want to do Jane Austen justice,” she says. “I think it’s time to have our version of a human story, and see this level of intimacy between the sisters and have a new take on it. It’s important to keep reworking these stories. Jane Austen’s books are so timeless and so relevant today, and hopefully we reach a new audience as well with our film.”

schema.headline: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Costume Designer on Blending Historical Accuracy and Modern Styling for the Dashwood Sisters: ‘We Want to Do Jane Austen Justice’

title: KJ Apa on Becoming Jimmy Stewart, Speculation That He Is the Singer Mr. Fantasy and Opening Up About His Addictions and Recovery: ‘This Is A Huge Part of Who I Am’
description:

	“I was watc
body:
When KJ Apa was being considered to star as Jimmy Stewart in the new biopic “Jimmy,” he took another look at “It’s a Wonderful Life.”

	“I was watching and thinking, how am I going to pull this off?” the actor, who is best known for his starring role as Archie in the CW coming-of-age series “Riverdale,” tells me. “I don’t look anything like him. I don’t sound anything like him. I’m not as tall as him. Like none of it lined up, but by the end of the movie, I was like, ‘I have to do it.’”
	

	“Jimmy,” directed by Aaron Burns, chronicles Stewart’s rise in Hollywood and time fighting in WWII. After winning an Oscar for “The Philadelphia Story” in 1941, he was drafted to serve in the war. Rather than use his celebrity clout to dodge the draft, Stewart enlisted and flew 20 missions over Europe and rose to the rank of colonel.


	When he returned home from the war, however, Hollywood seemed to have forgotten about him. Stewart considered moving back home to Indiana, Pennsylvania to work in his father’s general store. But Frank Capra convinced him to star as George Bailey in what is now considered one of the greatest films of all time, the 1946 Christmas classic “It’s a Wonderful Life.”

	“Frank Capra gave him that script and he was going through a lot of what George Bailey was going through,” said Apa, who will receive a Spotlight Award on Oct. 18 at the Newport Beach Film Festival. “I honestly think ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ was like therapy for him. He was able to continue in his career. His daughter Kelly told me when he came back from the war, he said he wasn’t sure if he was a retired actor or a retired pilot. He just didn’t know what he was doing. I think he was lost.”
	

	I sat down with Apa before the recent world premiere of “Jimmy” at the Heartland Film Festival in Indianapolis. We talked about finding Stewart’s voice, being open about his addictions and recovery and speculation that he is the singer Mr. Fantasy.

	Quick note: I make a brief cameo in the film as bandleader Glenn Miller.
	
		What did you know about Jimmy Stewart before signing on for the movie?	

	Growing up in New Zealand, I didn’t know much about old Hollywood. I wasn’t familiar with the old Hollywood movie stars.
	
		Take me through the process of getting Jimmy Stewart’s voice?	

	I was meant to shoot a movie called “The Sublime Biopic” about the band Sublime. [Apa was set to star as the band’s late frontman Bradley Nowell]. I was working with a dialect coach, Eliza Simpson, at the time and she’s phenomenal. I worked with her every second of every day for “Jimmy.” I watched all his films. I would listen to him over and over and over again. You just have to spend a lot of time listening and repeating, listening and repeating, listening and repeating.
	
		His voice is so specific and iconic. It’s not like you could practice by using it when you’re at Starbucks.	

	For “Sublime,” I would do that. I’d go out and I’d talk to people in the accent. No one would think that wasn’t my voice. You’re totally right with this one. I was in no man’s land for the duration of the prep. I had not shared it with anyone. I was terrified. My only sounding board was Eliza.
	
		What was it like shooting your first scene using Jimmy’s voice?	

	It was really nerve-wracking. It could go two ways. I realized it was such a fine line.
	
		You didn’t want to sound like an “SNL” skit.	

	Exactly, which, by the way, I did read some of the things online. They were pretty funny. But at the end of the day, it’s completely out of my control. I can only focus on what I’m doing with the actors that I’m working with and with Aaron. There’s only so much that I can control. If I look like a fool, I look like a fool. I did my best.



	

					KJ Apa as Jimmy Stewart and Max Casella as Frank Capra in “Jimmy.”
	


	
		What do you want people to learn about Jimmy Stewart from the movie?	

	I want people to have the same feeling I had when I first read the script, which was it was unimaginable for me to believe that he was such a highly decorated actor, and then served for over 20 years as a B-24 bomber pilot. He was involved with the D-Day invasion and then came back and did like 50-plus movies. Frank Capra gave him that script and he was going through a lot of what George Bailey was going through. I honestly think “It’s a Wonderful Life” was like therapy for him. He was able to continue in his career. His daughter Kelly told me when he came back from the war, he said he wasn’t sure if he was a retired actor or a retired pilot. He just didn’t know what he was doing. I think he was lost. But I want people to know what he did for this country.
	
	
		Has Mr. Fantasy seen the film?	

	I have to ask him, but I think Mr. Fantasy would love this movie because he is such a positive guy and it’s a movie that will make you feel good. It’s not political. It’s not controversial. It’s about a man who doesn’t do the easy thing. He does the thing that he feels is the right thing to do, which is to serve his country because his father did the same, and his father’s father did the same.



	

					Paris Hilton and Mr. Fantasy at the TikTok Awards 2025 in December.
									Billboard via Getty Images
	


	
		What do you say when people ask you if you’re Mr. Fantasy?	

	I say the truth, which is no. Listen, I wish that I could have the confidence to do what that guy does. I mean, he’s just so himself. The energy that guy has!
	
		This summer on Dylan Sprouse’s podcast “Wildmen,” you talked about your struggles with food. You’ve also been open about your addiction and recovery. Do you ever worry that you’re putting yourself out there too much?	

	It really doesn’t get more simple than that I’m a good friend of Dylan Sprouse. He asked me to come on his podcast. I had just dropped my son back off to his mum’s house. I was completely unprepared. I just rolled up and sat down, and we started talking, and I felt in that moment like, this is who I am. This is a huge part of who I am. These thoughts that go into an eating disorder or drug addiction or other addictions, they are all part of who I am and have taken up so much of my life. I’ve had so many people come up to me saying, “Thanks for sharing that.” I honestly didn’t realize that it would have that reaction. It was cool.

	“Jimmy” is in theaters on Nov. 6.

	This Q&A was edited for length and clarity.

schema.headline: KJ Apa on Becoming Jimmy Stewart, Speculation That He Is the Singer Mr. Fantasy and Opening Up About His Addictions and Recovery: ‘This Is A Huge Part of Who I Am’

title: Harry Styles ‘Together, Together’ Tour Doc Coming From John Wilson, Universal Pictures Content Group (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Harry Styles has invited one of the buzziest documentary filmmakers on the market behind the curtain of his historic Madison Square Garden residenc
body:
Harry Styles has invited one of the buzziest documentary filmmakers on the market behind the curtain of his historic Madison Square Garden residency.

	John Wilson, the director behind indie box-office surprise “The History of Concrete” and HBO’s “How To with John Wilson,” has been rolling cameras on Styles at MSG since August, two sources with knowledge of the project said.


	Wilson is capturing footage for a doc expected to be a hybrid of live performances and a glimpse into Styles’ world. One source described it as featuring authentic human stories of everyone involved in the tour —from the singer and his fans to countless others behind the scenes.
	

	Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures and Styles produced the project. UPCG will own global rights to the film. Though distribution plans are still being worked out, insiders said the doc may be positioned for a theatrical release via Universal.


	Styles is currently in the midst of the largest single-engagement residency ever at MSG, part of his “Together, Together” tour. It began in late August and is set to run through the end of October. The show has created plenty of viral moments and provided ample short-shorts. Reps for the singer, Wilson, and Universal had no immediate comment. Social media lit up over the weekend thanks to a fan-snapped photo of Wilson trailing styles with a camera.

	Wilson’s got a knack for interrogating the mundane, as well as highlighting the absurdity of humans and the levers that make them work. He may seem an out-of-the-box choice for a glossy pop music documentary, but not if you’re paying attention to current sensibilities. Look at Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, whose Elizabeth Holmes project “You Can See Everything” is burning up the specialty box office this weekend. Fielder started in the realm of absurdist comedy, and with the Holmes project moves into a world of watercooler high crimes and compelling fourth-wall breaking. Billie Eilish recruited “Titanic ” and “Avatar” mastermind James Cameron to direct her own theatrical concert opus “Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour,” which was released in theaters this summer. 
	

	Wilson began his career directing music videos. He is repped by UTA.

title: 'DWTS' Pro Val Chmerkovskiy Suspended From Show After Will Smith Slap Joke
description:
'Dancing with the Stars'
                          Pro Val Chmerkovskiy Suspended ...
body:
'Dancing with the Stars'
                          Pro Val Chmerkovskiy Suspended ...
                          After Making Will Smith Slap Joke About Judge
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 17, 2026
                            1:56 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 17, 2026
                                2:47 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Val Chmerkovskiy -- a fan-favorite professional dancer on "Dancing with the Stars" -- has been suspended from the show for one week ... after he made a joke implying he almost slapped a female judge, like Will Smith slapped Chris Rock at the Oscars.
      
    
            Here's the deal ... Val is married to Jenna Johnson -- another professional dancer on the show -- who was dinged by Carrie Ann Inaba for including a lift in her routine with actor Harry Shum Jr.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Val rushed to his wife's defense ... and did it by invoking the Smith slap -- saying online people almost saw the "Fresh Prince" come out after Carrie Ann criticized his better half. The brief post has since been deleted.
      

            As you can imagine ... Val's comment -- though not meant literally -- went over like a lead balloon with fans, who didn't like the idea of Val hitting a woman for judging his wife's dancing. Inaba responded to the comment online as well ... reportedly sharing a headline about Val's words alongside the caption, "So this is what we are doing now?"
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Val took responsibility for his comments, apologized to fans and to Carrie Ann directly ... but that wasn't enough for BBC Studios, which produces the show.
      
    
            The company stated Val's post was "inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show." They then announced they were suspending him.
      
    
            Val's partner -- Jenna Dewan -- still has to dance this week ... with Alan Bersten, who was eliminated earlier in the competition, stepping in to dance with her.
